explanations: luna: The section's M-W-T and H-Y-Y roots name death and life as distinct endpoints; this verse recounts being dead, then given life, then dying and being raised again, a concrete sequence unlike the condemned state that reaches neither endpoint. | terra: Human beings were dead, were given life, will die, and will be revived, laying out the divinely ordered endpoints from which the Fire's inmate is suspended.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss explains Pharaoh's “keeping your women alive” as sparing them; this verse recounts the same selective killing and preservation, giving the dictionary sense its Qur'anic scene. | terra: Pharaoh's people slaughter sons and يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, using life language in the source section's precise sense of sparing and keeping alive.
terra: After the thunderbolt death, the Israelites are raised again, matching the section's collapse-and-recovery edge of the death root.

luna: The section diagnoses preferring the near life over the afterlife; this verse says some have bought worldly life in exchange for the next and that their punishment will not be lightened, an exact choice-and-consequence parallel. | terra: Those who buy worldly life at the price of the Hereafter receive punishment that is not lightened, joining the wrong exchange to unrelieved torment.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y note equates a long remaining time with living; this verse says some wish for a thousand years of life, yet such length would not remove them from punishment, distinguishing duration from true enduring life. | terra: A thousand years of life would not move the covetous person away from punishment, proving that mere duration is not the beneficial, lasting life of the section.

luna: The section distinguishes mere non-death from real, enduring life; here those killed in God's way are explicitly said not to be dead but alive with God, a sharp contrary state. | terra: Those killed in God's way must not be called dead but alive, distinguishing hidden, beneficial life from biological appearance.

luna: The section's H-Y-W dictionary branch describes water reviving what it touches; this verse says rain revives the earth after its death, a natural scene that makes the water/life link visible. | terra: Water revives earth after its death and disperses living creatures, bringing the life root, water, and benefit into one sign.
terra: The followers wish for a return to disown their leaders, but they will not emerge from the Fire, another concrete denial of an endpoint to punishment.
luna: The section's H-Y-Y dictionary sense of life as benefit fits “in retribution there is life” (في القصاص حياة): the verse names a social good that preserves life, not just biological duration.
luna: The section centers on a person unable to pass into death or life; this verse describes a people made to die and then restored to life, a direct contrary passage through the two endpoints.
terra: God is the Living, the Sustainer, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes; perfect life without sleep sharply contrasts the inmate's denied, restorative sleep and empty nondeath.

luna: The section distinguishes death from a recoverable interval; this man is made dead for a hundred years and then raised, a full death-and-return boundary against the fire's refusal of either endpoint.

luna: The section describes people preferring the near life; this verse lists its adornments and says they are only worldly-life enjoyment while the good return is with God, exposing the short reach of those desires. | terra: Desirable worldly things are beautified as the enjoyment of this life, while the good return is with God, setting up the “better than this” offer in 3:15.
terra: Gardens and lasting divine approval are announced as better than the worldly attractions of 3:14, spelling out the section's better alternative.
terra: The condemned remain under the curse with punishment neither lightened nor delayed, specifying continued existence without relief.

luna: The section contrasts worldly life with the afterlife; this verse says one who seeks the reward of this world receives some of it, while one who seeks the reward of the afterlife receives it, making the chosen horizon explicit. | terra: The ayah separates whoever wants worldly reward from whoever wants the reward of the Hereafter, casting the section's preference as an actionable intention.
terra: At Uḥud some desired worldly gain and others desired the Hereafter, a concrete enactment of the preference diagnosed in 87:16.
terra: After distress, drowsiness descends as security upon part of the believers, showing sleep as a restorative good unavailable in the section's punishment.

luna: The section asks what counts as life beyond bodily survival; here the slain are alive with their Lord and provided for, unlike the torment that has neither death nor beneficial life. | terra: The slain are alive with their Lord and provided for, coupling true life with benefit and provision rather than mere continuance.
terra: Every soul tastes death, full recompense comes later, and worldly life is deceptive enjoyment; ordinary death and the near life's false value are held together.

luna: The section says the fire's victim cannot die and so cannot leave the torment; here burned skin is replaced so the punishment can continue. That is a specific bodily mechanism for sustained torment, though the verse does not use the no-death formula. | terra: Burned skins are repeatedly replaced so punishment can continue to be tasted, a concrete mechanism for torment that neither benefits as life nor concludes in death.
terra: Those who exchange worldly life for the Hereafter are told to fight, presenting the saving inverse of preferring the nearer life.

luna: The section's selection is between near life and afterlife; this verse calls worldly enjoyment little and says the afterlife is better for the one who is mindful, specifying the measure behind that choice. | terra: Worldly enjoyment is declared little and the Hereafter better for the God-conscious, a close verbal counterpart to 87:16-17.

luna: The section says the afterlife is better and more enduring than worldly life; this verse asks who seeks worldly reward and answers that with God is the reward of both this world and the next, placing worldly gain against the fuller source of reward.
luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss calls life a benefit; this verse says saving one person is like saving all humankind, making the value of preserving life explicit.
terra: The Fire's people want to leave but cannot and have lasting punishment, joining denied escape to the section's destructive permanence.

luna: The section contrasts the near life with what lasts; this verse calls worldly life only play and amusement and says the next life's home is better for the God-fearing, giving the same valuation. | terra: Worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter's home is better for the mindful, a concise valuation parallel to 87:16-17.

luna: The section's M-W-T dictionary includes sleep as death-like; this verse says God takes people at night and raises them by day, a recurring Qur'anic formulation of sleep followed by return. | terra: God takes people by night and raises them by day until their appointed term, a direct Quranic pattern behind the source's sleep-as-death sense.

luna: The section defines life as benefit and good; here a person is first dead, then given life and light by which to walk among people, making beneficial guidance a concrete opposite of the fire-dweller's lack of life. | terra: One who was dead is made alive and given light, opposite one trapped in darkness unable to emerge; this moral life has the usefulness missing from the section's Fire.
terra: Human beings live on earth, die there, and are brought out from it, a complete ordinary sequence against which the Fire's blocked death and life stand out.
terra: Heavy clouds deliver water and fruit from dead country, then the scene is explicitly compared with bringing out the dead.
terra: Pharaoh vows to kill the Israelites' sons and يَسْتَحْيِي their women, again making “give life” mean leave alive under selective extermination.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y dictionary gloss says Pharaoh's “keeping women alive” means preserving them; Moses recalls that same policy here, where sons were killed and women spared. | terra: The recalled oppression pairs slaughtering sons with يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, exactly illustrating the dictionary sense of preserving someone alive.

luna: The section's M-W-T dictionary entry describes being struck down and then recovering; Moses falls unconscious (خر موسى صعقا) and then wakes (أفاق), a precise Qur'anic scene parallel to that recoverable state. | terra: Moses falls stricken and then, when he recovers, speaks; the sequence matches the source dictionary's “moutah” as a collapse from which one later regains consciousness.
terra: Later heirs seize the goods of “this nearer/lower” life while presuming forgiveness, using أَدْنَى for the morally chosen immediate gain.
terra: God covers the believers with drowsiness as security, another specific instance of sleep conveying protection and benefit.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss says life means benefit and good; the command to answer God and the Messenger “to what gives you life” (لما يحييكم) presents guidance as life-giving benefit. | terra: Believers are told to answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives them life, exemplifying the section's definition of life as benefit and good.
terra: الدُّنْيَا names the nearer side of the valley, preserving the literal spatial nearness from which the source section says worldly life receives its name.
terra: Some desire the goods of this world while God desires the Hereafter for them, setting immediate acquisition against the divinely valued destination.

luna: The section says people prefer near life over the afterlife; this rebuke asks whether they are content with worldly life “instead of” the next, then calls its enjoyment little, making the preference and its scale explicit. | terra: The question “Are you content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter?” names the same preference and declares worldly enjoyment slight by comparison.
terra: The hypocrites would follow for a near gain and easy journey; this is a specific instance of visible nearness winning preference, though it does not explicitly contrast the two lives.

luna: The section describes people choosing the near life over the afterlife; this verse identifies those satisfied with worldly life and heedless of God's signs, the stance that leads into the fire named in 10:8. | terra: Those content and at ease with worldly life do not expect the meeting with God, specifying the stance behind the section's preference.

luna: The section connects preference for worldly life with the fire's dead-end condition; this verse gives the consequence for the heedless in 10:7, making Hell their abode for what they earned. | terra: Fire is the refuge earned by the worldly contentment described in 10:7, completing the same choice and destination as 87:16 and 87:13.

luna: The section contrasts near worldly life with what lasts, and 87:4–5 shows pasture turning to dark debris; this verse explicitly likens worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that dries and is carried away, repeating that passing scene. | terra: Worldly life is rain, mingled growth, sudden ruin, and a field as if it had not flourished yesterday; the scene makes the near life's passing character visible.
terra: The wrongdoers are told to taste “the punishment of permanence,” directly naming the destructive lastingness distinguished from true lasting life.
terra: God gives life and causes death, and all return to Him; the repeated formula confirms that both transitions and their destination belong to one Lord.

luna: The section says choosing the near life leaves the lasting afterlife; this verse describes people who want worldly life and its adornment and receive their deeds' full measure in this life, with 11:16 stating what they lack afterward. | terra: Those who desire worldly life and its adornment may receive their works in it, isolating the near reward they chose.

luna: This continuation of 11:15 says such people have nothing in the afterlife except Fire and that their works come to nothing, a direct consequence for the worldly-life choice developed in the section. | terra: For the people of 11:15, nothing awaits in the Hereafter but Fire and their works collapse, showing the near life's apparent benefit ending in the section's nonlife.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y root describes being left alive rather than wiped out; this verse values the lawful remainder of a transaction over cheating, showing how “what remains” can be a remnant of provision, not a lifespan. | terra: “The remainder from God is better” joins بَقِيَّة and خَيْرٌ in one phrase, closely matching the section's claim that good is what truly remains.
terra: The wretched are in the Fire with anguished breathing, opening a passage that compares the two kinds of continued afterlife existence.
terra: The Fire's people abide there for the divinely appointed span, making explicit the punitive staying developed by the section.
terra: The blessed abide in the Garden and receive a gift that is not cut off, the beneficial permanence opposite the Fire's barren continuance in 11:106-107.
terra: The question asks why earlier generations lacked “people of remainder” who restrained corruption, joining the ب ق ي root to preserved moral good.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss calls life benefit and good, while its B-Q-Y gloss turns on what remains; this verse says flood scum disappears but what benefits people remains on earth, joining those two roots in a precise image of enduring benefit. | terra: Flood foam disappears while what benefits people remains on earth; benefit and remaining meet here exactly as the section's definitions of life and lastingness require.

luna: The section contrasts worldly life with the lasting next life; this verse says people rejoice in worldly life while its enjoyment is little compared with the afterlife, making the difference in duration explicit.

luna: The section explains that al-dunyā is the near life preferred over the more lasting one; this verse describes people who prefer worldly life over the afterlife and turn from God's path, a direct moral counterpart. | terra: Those who love worldly life over the Hereafter enact the same preference as 87:16 and bend others away from God's path.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y dictionary note glosses “they keep your women alive” as sparing them; Moses recalls Pharaoh's killing the sons while keeping the women alive, the exact survival sense the section names. | terra: Moses recalls Pharaoh's slaughter of sons and يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, the same survival sense of the life root cited by the section.

luna: The section's wording “neither dies nor lives” meets the image of death reaching the wrongdoer from every side while “he is not dead” (وما هو بميت); the verse makes the blocked release concrete. | terra: Death comes to the tyrant from every direction yet he is not dead, making concrete the section's state in which torment removes life's good without completing death.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and remains as inheritor, joining divine control of both endpoints to what remains when creatures pass.

luna: The section's central phrase suspends a person between death and life; this verse calls the things invoked besides God dead, not living, providing the clear dead pole for comparison while its own context concerns powerless idols. | terra: The invoked beings are “dead, not living,” an exact lexical reversal that distinguishes lifeless nonentities from the section's conscious state that is neither completed death nor true life.
terra: Those who do good receive good here, but the home of the Hereafter is better, locating goodness fully in the destination the section calls better and more lasting.

luna: The section names a dictionary sense in which water gives life; here water from the sky revives earth after its death, another direct Qur'anic formulation of that relation. | terra: Water from heaven revives earth after death, a direct recurring form of water as the bearer of life.

luna: The section's M-W-T gloss defines death as strength departing and its H-Y-Y gloss ties life to benefit; this verse says some are returned to feeblest old age and lose knowledge after having it, depicting diminished capacity before death. | terra: Some are returned to the feeblest age and lose former knowledge, an earthly case in which life's biological continuation no longer guarantees retained power or benefit.
terra: When wrongdoers see punishment, it is neither lightened nor postponed, closing both relief and delay as exits from the section's nonlife.
terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, a direct formulation of the section's passing-near versus lasting choice.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss defines life as benefit and good; this verse promises “a good life” (حياة طيبة) to believing doers, giving positive content to the life denied in 87:13. | terra: Faithful good action is answered with “a good life,” explicitly uniting life with goodness against the useless continuance described in the Fire.

luna: The section's central diagnosis is preferring worldly life over the afterlife; this verse uses that precise contrast for those who have loved the worldly life over the next, tying the choice to disbelief. | terra: Loving worldly life more than the Hereafter is given as the reason for rejection, an explicit parallel to the section's diagnosis of preference.

luna: The section contrasts the near life with the lasting afterlife; this verse distinguishes the person who wants the immediate world and is given some of it from the one who seeks the next life in 17:19. | terra: Whoever wants the immediate life may receive some of it, then is assigned Hell; “the immediate” restates the nearness contained in الدُّنْيَا.

luna: The section presents the afterlife as the lasting alternative to near-world preference; this verse names the believer who seeks the next life and strives for it, supplying the other side of the choice introduced in 17:18. | terra: Whoever wants the Hereafter and strives for it in faith has an appreciated effort, the positive choice set against 17:18's immediate life and Hell.
terra: The cave sleepers look awake though they are asleep and are physically turned, staging sleep as a deathlike state without completed death.
terra: The sleepers are “raised,” then ask how long they remained, joining recovery from deathlike sleep to the section's language of staying.

luna: The section calls this world's life near and contrasts it with what lasts; this verse pictures worldly life as rain-grown plants that dry and scatter, a concrete image of transience that also recalls 87:4–5. | terra: Worldly life is rain-fed vegetation that becomes dry matter scattered by wind, supplying the vanishing side for the lasting deeds of 18:46.

luna: The section contrasts the near world's life with what is more lasting; this verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says the “lasting good deeds” (الباقيات الصالحات) are better with the Lord. | terra: Worldly wealth and children are adornment, but “the lasting righteous deeds” are better in reward and hope, joining the section's خَيْرٌ and أَبْقَىٰ logic.
terra: Believers who do good receive the Gardens of Paradise as hospitality, introducing beneficial afterlife continuance rather than mere survival.
terra: They abide in Paradise and desire no transfer from it, the fulfilled permanence opposite the Fire's inhabitants who plead for an end or exit.

luna: The section describes the afterlife as better and more lasting; this verse calls lasting righteous deeds (والباقيات الصالحات) better as reward and return with the Lord. | terra: “The lasting righteous deeds” are better in reward and return, repeating the section's union of goodness and permanence.

luna: The section introduces the magicians' prostration and confession before Pharaoh's threat in 20:71; this verse is the act of prostration itself, linking the section's prayer-and-purification choice to the later refusal to trade faith for near life. | terra: The magicians fall in prostration and affirm the Lord of Aaron and Moses; this act identifies the speakers whose worldly-life refusal leads to 20:74-76.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y root note links “more enduring” with lasting life; Pharaoh uses أَبْقَىٰ for the punishment he threatens after the magicians' prostration (20:70), exposing his claim to endurance against the section's true afterlife measure. | terra: Pharaoh claims that his punishment is harsher and more lasting, appropriating أَبْقَىٰ for a mortal threat that the magicians answer with God's permanence.

luna: The section says people prefer the near life over the lasting one; the magicians answer that they will not prefer Pharaoh over the clear proofs and say he can rule only “this worldly life” (هذه الحياة الدنيا), showing the choice under immediate threat. | terra: The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh and limit his power to “this worldly life,” exposing the boundary of the punishment he had called lasting in 20:71.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y root and 87:17's “more enduring” meet the magicians' answer to Pharaoh: “Allah is better and more enduring” (والله خير وأبقى). This is their explicit correction of his boast in 20:71. | terra: The magicians declare God “better and more lasting,” answering Pharaoh's أَبْقَىٰ and anticipating the exact pairing of 87:17.

luna: The section's wording at 87:13, “neither dies nor lives,” is repeated here for the criminal who meets his Lord; the same fire context makes the suspended state a stated outcome of judgment. | terra: The magicians state the section's sentence exactly: the criminal has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; their warning turns Pharaoh's threat into the choice's final horizon.

luna: The section contrasts the fire-bound with the purified person's lasting outcome; this neighboring promise says a believer who comes with good deeds receives the high degrees, giving the positive side before 20:76 names the gardens. | terra: Coming to God as a believer with righteous deeds yields the highest ranks, supplying the living positive destination opposite the criminal's nonlife in 20:74.

luna: The section names the purified person's lasting afterlife as the counterpart to the fire; this continuation promises Eden gardens, abiding there, as “the reward of whoever purifies himself” (جزاء من تزكى). | terra: Eternal gardens are the reward of the one who purifies himself; this places the purification of 87:14 directly beside the lasting-life contrast of 20:74.
terra: At resurrection the guilty whisper that they remained only ten days, exposing the nearer life's apparent length as brief from the lasting side.
terra: The most perceptive say they remained only a day, intensifying the collapse of worldly duration begun in 20:103.

luna: The section calls out a false offer of permanence; Satan's “tree of eternity” and kingdom that does not decay (شجرة الخلد وملك لا يبلى) is the counterfeit lasting life against which 87:17's afterlife is measured. | terra: Satan offers Adam “the tree of immortality” and a kingdom that does not decay, the section's counterfeit promise of lasting life.
terra: Turning from God's reminder brings a constricted living, a life-form whose deprivation helps distinguish biological duration from beneficial life.

luna: The section's D-N-W note says the world is named for nearness and its B-Q-Y note for lasting; this verse calls worldly provision a flower and says what is with the Lord is “better and more enduring” (خير وأبقى). | terra: The flower of worldly life is a test, whereas the Lord's provision is “better and more lasting,” almost restating 87:16-17.
terra: Earlier messengers ate food and were not immortal, setting bodily life and its needs within a mortal limit despite prophetic rank.

luna: The section's secondary H-Y-W gloss joins water with the revival of whatever it touches; this verse says every living thing was made from water, giving a distinct Qur'anic water-and-life relation without claiming the same Paradise setting. | terra: Every living thing is made from water, a Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's life-giving water called al-ḥayawān.

luna: The section sets real endurance against a false promise of immortality; this verse says no human before Muhammad was granted eternal life, bounding the promise of Satan's “tree of eternity” in 20:120. | terra: No human before the Prophet was granted immortality; earthly death is universal, so indefinite continuation cannot make the nearer life permanent.
terra: Every soul tastes death before being returned to God, a universal mortal boundary that makes Hell's refusal to complete death exceptional.

luna: The section's water-and-life dictionary sense is echoed when rain makes barren earth stir, swell, and grow every kind; the verse itself uses that scene to establish resurrection, joining provision to life after lifelessness. | terra: The ayah moves through human life, death, powerless old age, and rain that makes lifeless earth stir and grow, gathering several of the section's distinctions between force, life, and revival.

luna: The section's fire-dwellers have no release through death; here every attempt to leave Hell from anguish is met by return to it, a separate but concrete form of being unable to escape the condition. | terra: Each attempt to leave the Fire from anguish returns its people to it, showing continued existence without the release of death.
terra: After the stages of earthly creation, human beings will die, marking death as a true transition rather than the endless attenuation described in the Fire.
terra: After death people are raised on Resurrection Day, completing the sequence whose endpoints 87:13 deliberately denies within Hell.
luna: The section says the hereafter is the lasting life; these speakers deny it and claim there is only worldly life, “we die and live” (نموت ونحيا), a direct contrary account of the endpoints.
terra: God gives life and causes death alongside the alternation of night and day, embedding the two endpoints in an ordered cycle rather than random loss.

luna: The section quotes the post-judgment regret for not having sent ahead for one's life; here, when death comes, the speaker asks to be sent back so he can do right, the same regret framed as an impossible return.

luna: This verse answers the return request in 23:99 with a barrier until resurrection, giving a specific boundary between death and renewed earthly life that sharpens the section's missed-life regret.
terra: God asks how many years people remained on earth, forcing the condemned to measure the life they preferred against their present destination.
terra: They answer that they remained a day or part of a day, recognizing the nearer life's brevity.
terra: God confirms that they remained only a little, if they had known, making their former preference a failure of temporal judgment.

luna: The section names a H-Y-W branch associating water with life; this verse says God created every moving creature from water, a specific creation-side counterpart to the dictionary's water-that-revives sense.
terra: Cast into a constricted place in the Fire, its people call for destruction, seeking an end rather than the suspended continuance described by the section.
terra: They are told to call not for one destruction but many, intensifying the impossible wish for extinction begun in 25:13.

luna: The section's sleep gloss and its exclusion of sleep in the fire meet this verse's pairing of sleep as repose with daytime rising (والنوم سباتا وجعل النهار نشورا), a normal cycle withheld from the condemned. | terra: Sleep is made repose and daytime “resurrection,” presenting waking as return from a deathlike interval.
terra: The wind and purifying water introduce the life-giving act of 25:49, contributing the water itself rather than the following ayah's revival.

luna: The section's secondary H-Y-W dictionary sense describes water in Paradise reviving what it touches; this verse says rain is sent to revive a dead land and provide drink for people and animals, a direct water-gives-life scene with provision as its benefit. | terra: Purifying rain gives life to a dead land and drink to creatures, directly paralleling the source dictionary's water that imparts life.

luna: The section's life-and-endurance contrast is sharpened by the command to rely on “the Living who does not die” (الحي الذي لا يموت); God's unending life is unlike the condemned person's state of neither living nor dying. | terra: God is “the Living who does not die”; His deathlessness is perfect life, sharply distinguishing it from the Fire's inmate who does not die yet also does not live.
terra: The servants of the Merciful abide in the lofty chambers, which are praised as a good settlement and residence; goodness and staying coincide there.

luna: The section's death-and-life roots are paired by Abraham's declaration that God “causes me to die, then gives me life” (يميتني ثم يحيين); it assigns both endpoints to God rather than to a trapped intermediate state. | terra: Abraham assigns both his death and subsequent revival to his Lord, placing the two endpoints denied in Hell under divine agency.
terra: After Noah and those with him are saved, “the remaining ones” are drowned, using ب ق ي for those left behind who are then eradicated.
terra: The people build monumental structures as though they might live forever, exposing worldly works aimed at counterfeit permanence.
terra: The Prophet cannot make the dead hear the call, using death for lost responsiveness and sharpening the section's beneficial sense of life.

luna: The section names the H-Y-Y sense “keep alive”; this verse says Pharaoh killed the sons of one group while sparing its women, a precise example of life preserved under oppression. | terra: Pharaoh slaughters sons and يَسْتَحْيِي women, showing life as being spared from eradication rather than as flourishing.

luna: The section contrasts near-world enjoyment with what lasts; this verse says whatever was given is only worldly enjoyment and “what is with God is better and more lasting” (خير وأبقى). | terra: Whatever people receive is worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is “better and more lasting,” the section's two lives stated as alternatives.
terra: One promised a good promise and meeting it is contrasted with one briefly furnished with worldly enjoyment and then brought to judgment.

luna: The section rebukes preferring worldly life over the enduring afterlife; this verse commands seeking the Hereafter through what God has given while not forgetting one's share of this world, adding a boundary that the choice concerns priority rather than erasing worldly life. | terra: The command is to seek the home of the Hereafter with God's gift while not forgetting one's worldly share, defining a boundary between proper use and preference.
terra: Those desiring worldly life wish for Qārūn's visible fortune, dramatizing how the near good attracts preference.
terra: People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and good action, correcting the worldly desire voiced in 28:79.
terra: Everything is perishing except God's face, a comprehensive boundary between created continuance and the permanence the section values.
terra: Every soul tastes death and then returns to God, repeating the ordinary passage from nearer life to the lasting destination.

luna: The section's Paradise-water gloss turns on water restoring life; this verse has the questioners acknowledge that God sends rain and revives the earth after its death, a repeated but distinct earthly instance. | terra: Rain revives earth after its death, again placing life-giving water against lifelessness.

luna: The section quotes this verse's claim that the afterlife is “the true life” (لهي الحيوان), grounding its contrast between the near life and lasting life in an explicit Qur'anic formulation. | terra: The worldly life is diversion and play while the Hereafter is al-ḥayawān, the true life; this is the section's lexical claim that real life belongs to what lasts.

luna: The section explains that people choose the near life; this verse says they know only the outward aspect of worldly life while heedless of the afterlife, describing the narrowed perception behind that preference. | terra: People know only the outward appearance of worldly life while remaining heedless of the Hereafter, explaining how nearness hides the lasting life.

luna: The section's H-Y-W dictionary branch links water and revival; this verse places rain that revives earth after its death among God's signs, giving the same life-after-death relation in a different scene. | terra: Heavenly water revives earth after death within a catalogue of signs, repeating the section's water-life association.

luna: The section's secondary H-Y-W dictionary sense describes water that revives what it touches; this verse asks the reader to see God revive earth after its death and says He is the reviver of the dead, a close Qur'anic image of life after non-life. | terra: God's mercy revives the earth after its death, and the ayah explicitly carries that act over to reviving the dead.
terra: The same inability to make the dead hear recurs, marking receptive hearing as a form of life beyond biological duration.

luna: The section's M-W-T root gloss centers on strength leaving; this verse traces humans from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, showing a loss of force within life rather than the fire's blocked death. | terra: God creates from weakness, gives strength, then makes weakness follow strength; this bodily arc concretely displays the withdrawal of force used to define death in the section.
terra: When the Hour rises, the guilty swear they remained only an hour, showing worldly duration collapsing at resurrection.
terra: Those given knowledge correct them: they remained until the Day of Resurrection, distinguishing the measured nearer stay from the lasting reality now reached.
terra: Whenever the defiantly wicked seek to leave the Fire they are returned to it, another concrete form of the section's inescapable nonlife.
terra: Water is driven to barren land and brings forth crops eaten by people and animals, an indirect but concrete meeting of water, restored productivity, and benefit.

luna: The section's secondary water gloss describes revival by water; this verse has wind carry clouds, rain revive a dead town, and compares that revival to resurrection, making the life-after-death relation explicit. | terra: Winds raise clouds, rain revives dead land, and the ayah identifies this as the pattern of resurrection.
terra: The living and the dead are not equal, and responsiveness to hearing marks the difference; this supplies a moral sense of life beyond bodily duration.

luna: The section's phrase from 87:13 is almost fully restated: they are not brought to death and the fire's torment is not eased. This adds the explicit absence of relief to the same no-death condition. | terra: The Fire's people are neither finished by a decree of death nor relieved of punishment, the same suspended condition developed from 87:13.

luna: After the no-death and unrelieved torment in 35:36, the people ask to be brought out to do right, while the answer recalls that they were given a lifetime; this makes their lost chance at beneficial life concrete.
terra: Dead earth is revived and made to yield grain people eat, coupling restored life with concrete benefit.
terra: Those raised from graves call them their sleeping place, bringing sleep, death, and awakening into the same scene.
terra: Whomever God grants long life is reversed in creation, qualifying the assumption that more duration by itself is better life.
terra: The warning addresses whoever is alive while judgment becomes due against rejecters, using life for receptive capacity and making its benefit explicit.
terra: The skeptic displays decayed bones and asks who can give them life, turning loss of bodily power into an explicit challenge about restoration.
terra: The answer says the One who originated the bones will revive them, resolving 36:78's apparent extinction with divine life-giving power.
terra: The Garden's speaker asks whether they will die no more, setting up joyous permanence as the reverse of Hell's inability to die.
terra: “Except our first death, and we will not be punished” joins no further death to freedom from torment, precisely distinguishing paradise's deathlessness from 87:13.
terra: Noah and his family are rescued from great distress, supplying the act of preservation whose surviving descendants are named in 37:77.
terra: Noah's descendants are made “the survivors,” a direct Quranic instance of ب ق ي as preservation through threatened extinction.
terra: Rain-grown crops flourish, yellow, and become debris as a reminder, a concrete passing-life scene that supports the section's distinction between what fades and remains.

luna: The section's M-W-T dictionary note includes sleep as “death”; this verse says God takes souls at death and during sleep, then retains some and sends others back, clarifying why a recoverable sleep is unlike the fire-dweller's condition. | terra: God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining those decreed to die and returning the others; this directly realizes the source section's secondary death-as-sleep sense.
terra: One trumpet blast fells creation and the next makes them stand, placing collapse and recovery at the cosmic threshold of death and life.

luna: The section's life-and-death roots are paired in this confession by people already confronting judgment: they say God caused them to die twice and live twice, then admit their sins and ask for a way out. It gives a real sequence of endpoints against 87:13's suspended state. | terra: The condemned confess two deaths and two givings of life, recognizing the full sequence whose final punishment cannot be escaped by another death.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y note uses Pharaoh's sparing of women to explain “keep alive”; here Pharaoh orders the believers' sons killed and women spared, repeating the specific survival sense in another part of the Moses story. | terra: The command to kill believers' sons and يَسْتَحْيُوا their women repeats the section's “keep alive” sense within a renewed threat of extermination.

luna: The section's contrast between the near life and enduring hereafter is stated directly: worldly life is only temporary enjoyment, while the next life is “the abode of permanence” (دار القرار). | terra: The believing man calls worldly life only an enjoyment and the Hereafter the home of settled permanence, directly restating the section's temporal contrast.

luna: The section recalls Pharaoh boasting that his punishment would be more enduring; this verse says Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour's severe punishment, showing the lasting fate behind that boast.
terra: The Fire's people ask its keepers for even one day of reduced punishment, showing how continued time there lacks benefit or respite.

luna: The section's H-Y-Y gloss gives life the sense of benefit and good; this verse says the living and dead are not equal, alongside the contrast of the blind and seeing, using life and death for opposed responsiveness rather than the fire's intermediate state.
terra: God gives life and causes death by decisive command, reinforcing that the Fire's denied death is governed rather than accidental.
terra: The Fire is called the enemies of God's “home of permanence,” locating everlasting duration in the punitive counterpart to the Hereafter's true life.
terra: Rain makes humbled earth stir and swell, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead.

luna: The section says the near life can be preferred to the lasting one; this verse distinguishes the person who seeks the harvest of the afterlife from one who seeks the harvest of this world and receives only some of it. | terra: The harvest metaphor divides desire for the Hereafter from desire for the worldly crop, and the latter yields no share in the Hereafter.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y gloss and 87:17 point to what endures; this verse calls what is with God better and more lasting than worldly enjoyment for those who believe and rely on their Lord. | terra: Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is “better and more lasting” for believers, exactly articulating the section's valuation.
terra: Measured water revives a dead land and becomes the stated likeness for human emergence from death.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y root names what remains; this verse says Abraham's declaration was made a “lasting word” (كلمة باقية) among his descendants, showing a different, transmitted form of endurance. | terra: Abraham leaves the declaration of God's oneness as “a word remaining” among his descendants, a constructive kind of survival through transmission.
terra: Worldly luxury is only temporary enjoyment, while the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the mindful, directly revaluing apparent benefit by permanence.
terra: The criminals abide in Hell's punishment, establishing the enduring scene whose desperate request receives the answer “you will remain” in 43:77.
terra: Punishment is not slackened and its people despair, specifying the absence of life's relief within the abiding scene of 43:74-77.

luna: The section cites the fire-dwellers asking for their Lord to end their condition; the answer “you will remain” (إنكم ماكثون) makes their continued confinement explicit and echoes the section's question of what it means to remain. | terra: The people of the Fire ask Mālik to have their Lord finish them, but are told they will remain, directly joining desired death to the section's terrible kind of staying.
terra: The sole God gives life and causes death and is Lord of present and former generations, extending His agency across every mortal span.

luna: The section's “does not die” wording can name either torment or true blessed life; here Garden-dwellers do not taste death there after the first death and are protected from Hell, separating joyful permanence from suspended punishment. | terra: The people of the Garden taste no death beyond the first death, making deathlessness the condition of true reward rather than the Fire's suspended nonlife.

luna: The section names water that revives what it touches; this verse includes rain reviving earth after its death among signs for people who reason, another direct formulation of that link. | terra: Provision descending from heaven revives earth after death, presenting life as bestowed nourishment and renewal.

luna: The section treats the afterlife as real and enduring; these speakers claim there is only worldly life and that time destroys them, a direct denial of the resurrection that gives the section's choice its stakes. | terra: The claim that there is only worldly life, in which “we die and live” and time destroys, is the false worldview that cannot see the section's real, later life.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and gathers everyone for the Day of Resurrection, correcting the worldly-only account of dying and living in 45:24.
terra: Paradise contains rivers of water that never alters, giving the source section's life-giving Paradise water a Quranic counterpart in unspoiled permanence.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion, reducing the object of preference to passing occupation rather than true life.
terra: Blessed water descends and grows gardens and grain, beginning the provision-and-revival sequence completed in 50:11.
terra: Tall palms with clustered fruit add the nourishment that makes the water's restored life beneficial before 50:11 names dead-land revival.

luna: After the rain and garden scene in 50:9–10, this verse calls the revived dead town provision for servants and says resurrection will likewise occur, connecting water-given life with the section's life-after-death image. | terra: Rain-fed provision gives life to a dead land and is made the image of emergence, uniting life, benefit, and resurrection.
terra: God gives life and causes death, and to Him is the destination, joining the endpoints to the final return.
terra: The verb دَنَا means “came near,” and may illuminate the source's derivation of الدُّنْيَا from nearness, though its revelatory scene does not itself concern worldly life's transience.

luna: The section places preference for worldly life beside remembering the Lord in 87:15; this verse describes one who turns away from the reminder and wants only “the life of this world” (الحياة الدنيا), joining the same two sides of the section's choice. | terra: The person who turns from remembrance wants only worldly life, joining rejection of reminder to the near-life preference that ends in loss.
terra: God is the one who causes death and gives life, a concise attribution of the two poles negated for the Fire's inmate.
terra: God destroyed Thamūd and “spared none,” using أَبْقَىٰ for the exact opposite of the source dictionary's plea to be left alive.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y note concerns what remains; this verse says all on earth pass away, setting up the boundary completed in 55:27 between transient life and what truly remains. | terra: Everyone upon the earth is passing away, naming the vanishing side of the section's contrast with what remains.

luna: The section's B-Q-Y root for remaining is explicit in the Lord's face “remaining” (ويبقى وجه ربك); it gives a source of permanence beyond the transient life set out in 55:26. | terra: The Lord's majestic face remains after all on earth passes in 55:26, giving permanence its absolute referent.
terra: The fruit of the two lasting gardens is دَانٍ, near at hand, showing that nearness itself can belong to the Hereafter and need not mean the transient الدُّنْيَا.
terra: God has apportioned death among people and cannot be outstripped, establishing death as a measured divine boundary rather than an escape available at will.
terra: God can replace people with their likes and create them in a form they do not know, completing 56:60's claim that continued existence and transformation remain His act.
terra: The possessor of all dominion gives life and causes death, grounding both states in the power that also determines permanence.
terra: God revives earth after its death, an explicit sign that life can be restored after apparent power has gone.

luna: The section divides worldly life from the enduring afterlife; this verse depicts worldly life as growth that yellows and becomes debris, and its pasture-like decay also recalls 87:4–5, giving the near life a concrete passing form. | terra: Worldly life is likened to rain-grown vegetation that withers into debris before the lasting outcomes of the Hereafter, joining the surah's passing growth to this section's choice.
terra: The Helpers يُؤْثِرُونَ others over themselves, using the section's preference verb for a saving, generous choice rather than preference for the nearer life.
terra: The death people flee will meet them before their return to the Knower, denying escape from the normal transition even as the condemned later seek death as release.
terra: God creates death and life as the field of testing, placing both endpoints under purposeful creation before the afterlife condition in which neither provides release.
terra: “Do you see any remnant of them?” uses بَاقِيَة after annihilation, matching the source dictionary's contrast between being spared and being eradicated.
terra: The successful person is in “a pleasing life,” a positive realization of the source definition that life entails benefit and good.
terra: Paradise has clusters دَانِيَة, brought near, relocating the section's nearness root inside the true lasting life.
terra: Faced with judgment, the condemned person wishes the first death had been final, voicing the desire for completion that the Fire refuses.
terra: Saqar “neither spares nor leaves,” a severe use of the section's ب ق ي sense: the fire consumes without granting its victim the completion of death.

luna: The section calls the present life al-dunyā and says people prefer it to what lasts; this verse rebukes loving the immediate life, beginning the same contrast completed in 75:21. | terra: “You love the immediate” expresses worldly preference through nearness rather than the noun الدُّنْيَا.

luna: This verse completes 75:20 by saying the immediate life is loved while the afterlife is left behind, a concise parallel to the section's near-life preference. | terra: “And leave the Hereafter” completes 75:20's choice in the same two-part form as 87:16-17.
terra: Garden shade is دَانِيَة over its people and fruit is lowered within reach, a concrete afterlife reversal of nearness as the worldly life's label.

luna: The section says people prefer the near life over the lasting afterlife; this verse similarly says people love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day, making the deferred consequence explicit. | terra: People love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty day, restating the section's near-life preference and its hidden consequence.

luna: The section notes that the M-W-T root can name sleep and says the fire-dweller has no sleep; this verse says sleep was made “rest” (سباتا), identifying the restorative pause absent from that condition. | terra: Sleep is made for rest, directly identifying the good contained in the deathlike interval that the Fire's inmate cannot enjoy.

luna: The section describes choosing the near life over the lasting one; this verse names the same choice as “preferring the worldly life” (وآثر الحياة الدنيا), directly identifying the orientation behind the outcome in 87:13. | terra: The transgressor “preferred the worldly life,” virtually repeating 87:16 and identifying the choice that produces the section's nonlife.

luna: The section links preference for worldly life to the fire's no-death condition; this verse supplies the immediate consequence for the preference in 79:38, “the Fire is the abode,” completing that parallel. | terra: This ayah gives Hell as the refuge of the person in 79:38, completing the same preference-to-Fire movement that the section draws from 87:16 back to 87:13.

luna: The section's opposite of preferring the near life is the successful, purified person; here the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire is set against the worldly-life chooser in 79:38.
luna: The section contrasts the fire's suspended torment with the lasting good afterlife; this verse completes 79:40 by making the Garden the abode of the one who restrained desire.
terra: The person given his record behind his back calls for destruction, voicing the condemned person's wish that death finish what judgment has begun.
terra: He enters a blazing fire after calling for destruction in 84:11, locating that impossible wish inside the section's punishment scene.

luna: The section quotes the regret “if only I had sent ahead for my life” (لحياتي); in this judgment scene the speaker recognizes too late that the life worth preparing for was the enduring one. | terra: At judgment the person wishes he had sent something ahead “for my life,” locating his real life after the nearer life, just as the section does.
luna: The section sets the fire-bound against the one who is purified; this verse says the most God-fearing will be kept far from the Fire, the direct reverse of the section's punishment scene.
luna: The section names purification as the outcome opposed to the fire; this verse describes the God-fearing person as giving wealth to purify himself, specifying the act behind that outcome.

luna: This verse says the giver does not act to repay anyone's favor; within the purification passage adjacent to 92:18, it clarifies that the deed is directed beyond worldly exchange, fitting the section's turn from near-life gain.
luna: The section's 87:15 pairs remembering the Lord with prayer; this verse says the giver seeks only the face of the Most High, specifying the orientation of the purified deed in 92:18.
luna: This verse concludes the same purification passage by promising that the God-fearing giver will be satisfied, the contented outcome opposite the Fire's no-life condition.
terra: The one whose scales are heavy is likewise in “a pleasing life,” the repeated positive counterpart to continued existence without good.
terra: The hoarder imagines his wealth has made him immortal, another false worldly permanence parallel to Satan's offer of the tree of immortality.
